How Turf is put together, so you can explain it when a user asks *what are you*, *how does this work*, or *what's the architecture*. This is the user-facing picture — the product, not the source tree.

## What Turf is

Turf is a **drop-in replacement for Terraform with agentic superpowers**. It speaks the language you already know — Terraform HCL and the public module registry — and runs the same **OpenTofu providers** to talk to clouds. What differs is the interface: instead of a `terraform apply` CLI aimed at a person, Turf exposes infrastructure management to an **AI agent** through the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**.

The desired state lives in the **configuration directory**: an ordinary Terraform root module. The user may have written it, or the agent writes it with its own file tools from a request in plain language. Either way every plan is a projection of the directory.

## Three pieces

### The MCP server (`turf-mcp-server`) — the interface

What the agent talks to: configuration discovery, workspaces, provider schemas, and Terraform's commands (`init`, `up`, `apply`, `destroy`, …) as MCP tools. One binary speaking MCP over **stdio** (default) or **HTTP**, so it plugs into any MCP client: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, [cagent](https://github.com/docker/cagent), [kagent](https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent) in Kubernetes, IDE extensions, or your own.

### The Turf engine — where plans are made and applied

Planning and applying happen in the **Turf engine**, a separate process the server drives. The engine reads the same configuration directory the agent edits, holds the state lock, runs the providers, and carries each **convergence** — rounds of plan → approve → apply until nothing is deferred — **durably**. A convergence lives in the engine, so a rollout survives a server restart, a dropped client and the end of the conversation: `open` reports one still in flight, and `apply` takes it up where it stands.

**Where the engine runs.** Unless `TURF_RESTATE_URL` names one, the server uses this user's **local engine**: on a Mac, the `turf` Homebrew service (`brew services start turf`), or `turf-mcp-server engine run` in a terminal. The server connects to it and never starts it. `turf-mcp-server engine status` reports where it listens, its processes, versions and logs. It listens only where this user's account can reach it, so a client in a container or another account cannot use it. `init`, the provider tools and the skills work without an engine; everything that plans needs one.

**One line.** A server drives a local engine of its own line (the same major and minor version, any patch) and refuses another, naming both versions; the refusal says which side is older. An older engine (the binaries were upgraded, the service was not restarted): restart it — `brew services restart turf`, or stop and start `turf-mcp-server engine run` where Homebrew does not run it. A convergence waiting in it is cancelled by the upgrade (the stack runs the old line's engine beside the new one until what was in flight there has finished); what was applied is kept, `apply` on it answers `cancelled` naming the upgrade, and `up` again plans over it. A newer engine: start the client again, so it runs the new server.

### The Turf CLI — a convenience wrapper

The **Turf CLI** launches `turf-mcp-server` as a subprocess over stdio and drives it through an embedded agent runtime, adding a `chat` REPL, `up`/`destroy` commands, session memory and a friendlier tool picker. It talks to the server only through MCP. It is a convenience, not a requirement.

```
You ──▶ MCP client ──(MCP)──▶ turf-mcp-server ──▶ Turf engine ──▶ OpenTofu providers ──▶ cloud
        (Claude, the Turf         the interface       durable         real plugins
         CLI, cagent, kagent…)                        plan/apply
```

## What the server exposes over MCP

- **Tools** — Terraform's commands: **configuration** (`init`, which also installs modules and providers), **workspaces** (`open`/`close`/`list`/`status`/`delete`), the **convergence** (`up` → review the vended plan → `apply`, with `destroy`, `refresh`, `import` and `invoke` as `up` in other modes, and `cancel`), **reading** (`show`, `output`, `state_list`), **state edits** (`taint`/`untaint`) and **providers** (`provider_search`/`describe`). There are no authoring tools: the configuration is files the agent edits, plus `*.turf.hcl` overlays for Turf's interaction points.
- **Skills** — how-to guides delivered as zero-argument tools: [`skill_deployment`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/) (running a configuration; load it first), [`skill_authoring`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/) (writing one) and [`skill_guide`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/) (use-case walkthroughs), plus `read_skill_file` for the reference files a skill names. *This document is one of those files.*
- **Prompts** — workflows a client offers as slash commands: `/up` (deploy or reconcile), `/destroy` (tear down) and `/guide` (a walkthrough).
- **Resources** — live, read-only views, updated as convergences move: `turf://workspaces` (the open workspaces and the convergence holding each), `turf://workspaces/{alias}`, `turf://workspaces/{alias}/convergences/{id}` (where it stands, the plan it waits on, every round), `…/rounds/{round}/plan` and `turf://workspaces/{alias}/state` (both redacted unless `?show_sensitive=true`).

## How it relates to Terraform and OpenTofu

- **Same inputs.** Terraform HCL and the public module registry work unchanged, with the divergences [`references/divergences.md`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/divergences/) lists.
- **Same providers.** Real OpenTofu providers make the create, read, update and delete calls; Turf orchestrates them.
- **Interoperable outputs.** The plan is OpenTofu's json-format plan, exactly as `tofu show -json` prints it, so policy engines (OPA/Conftest), security scanners and terraform-docs consume it directly. Every approval point vends it as a resource (`plan.uri`), which `show` reads.

The agentic layer sits around these standard pieces; it does not fork the semantics. Terraform knowledge transfers, and the artifacts stay interoperable.
